title: Escalation: TP timeouts/hangs in Dedicated (eu-west) — mitigation + rollout plan
summary: ArborPay escalated intermittent request timeouts and occasional “stuck” streaming responses on their eu-west Dedicated cluster when tensor parallel (TP=4) is enabled under peak concurrency. Redwood recapped current understanding (likely TP group stall driven by cancellation + barrier interaction and/or NCCL async errors not surfacing), reviewed immediate mitigations (traffic shaping, lowering concurrent streams, worker recycling, config flags), and aligned on an expedited canary/hotfix rollout plan for runtime 1.19 TP-stability changes (TP-group watchdog/quarantine + improved async error checks + cancellation-safe barriers). Redwood committed to delivering an RC build, a canary procedure, and a shared set of success metrics/rollback triggers. Customer requested clarity on operational impact, expected false positives from watchdog, and whether this requires node restarts.
topics: Impact recap (timeouts/5xx, stuck streams) and blast radius
Observed patterns: peak load, mixed sequence lengths, streaming disconnects
Canary plan: staged enablement and rollback criteria
questions: Can we canary the fix on a subset of workers without full cluster restart?
What metrics definitively tell us it’s comm stall vs kernel stall vs scheduler starvation?
If the watchdog triggers, does it kill only the TP group, the whole worker, or the node?
What’s the expected false positive rate and how do we tune sensitivity for streaming workloads?
action_items: Redwood (Dev Patel): Send ArborPay the current recommended mitigation flags + a short runbook for incident response in Dedicated (ETA today).
Redwood (Connor O'Brien): Provide runtime 1.19.1-rc build details and upgrade steps for Dedicated, including rollback procedure (ETA tomorrow).
Redwood (Rafael Mendes): Share proposed canary success metrics + alert thresholds (watchdog triggers, TP group resets, p95/p99 latency, timeout rate) (ETA tomorrow).
Customer (Miguel Santos): Provide a 2-hour window next week for canary during moderate traffic, plus current autoscaler/concurrency settings (ETA Monday).
Customer (Elena Popov): Share two representative workload profiles (prompt/seq length distributions + streaming vs non-streaming split) for Redwood to replay in stress harness (ETA Monday).
Redwood (Sofia Ivanova): Confirm whether their observed stuck streams align with the cancellation/barrier deadlock signature; request specific log lines and timestamps (ETA today).
next_steps: Redwood to send mitigation flags + checklist today.
Schedule 30-min canary kickoff early next week (Redwood + ArborPay SRE).
Deploy runtime 1.19.1-rc to 10% of Dedicated workers in eu-west, monitor for 24 hours, then expand to 50% if stable.
If stable and watchdog triggers remain below agreed threshold, proceed to full rollout and close escalation with post-incident write-up.
transcript:
Fireflies.ai Meeting Transcript

Title: Escalation: TP timeouts/hangs in Dedicated (eu-west) — mitigation + rollout plan
Date: 2025-02-27
Time: 17:00 UTC
Duration: 47 min

Attendees
Redwood Inference: Dev Patel, Rafael Mendes, Sofia Ivanova, Owen Phillips, Connor O'Brien
ArborPay: Nina Kaur, Miguel Santos, Elena Popov, Chris Hammond


Summary (auto-generated)
- Customer reports increased timeouts and some streams hanging under TP load.
- Redwood reviewed mitigations and proposed an RC canary plan for runtime fixes.
- Next steps agreed for logs, canary window, and rollout gates.

Topics (auto-generated)
1. Incident recap
2. Mitigation and config
3. Hotfix/canary rollout
4. Metrics and support follow-up


[00:00] Dev Patel (Redwood): Alright, we’ll get started. Nina, Miguel, Elena, Chris—thanks for joining on short notice. I’m Dev from support escalation. I’ve also got Rafael from SRE and Sofia from the runtime scheduling team. Connor’s here for release coordination.

[00:17] Nina Kaur (Customer): Thanks, Dev. Yeah, this has been pretty rough this week.

[00:22] Dev Patel (Redwood): Totally. Goal for today: (1) align on what we think is happening, (2) confirm immediate mitigations to reduce impact, and (3) agree on a canary plan for the TP stability fixes we’ve been working on.

[00:36] Miguel Santos (Customer): Sounds good.

[00:39] Dev Patel (Redwood): Quick recap from the ticket thread—this is your Dedicated eu-west cluster, TP equals four on the larger model route, and the symptom is request timeouts plus sometimes streaming responses that just… stop, right?

[00:54] Elena Popov (Customer): Yep. The stream starts and then you get like, some tokens and then it just stalls. Client is still connected. No more chunks.

[01:02] Chris Hammond (Customer): And separately we see spikes of 5xx from your gateway. But the most painful is the stuck streams because they tie up our app workers.

[01:12] Rafael Mendes (Redwood): Do you have a rough rate? Like how frequent at peak?

[01:16] Miguel Santos (Customer): Peak it was like… maybe 0.6 to 0.8% of requests timing out. Streams stall was lower but noisy—maybe 0.1%? It clusters during the morning EU traffic.

[01:28] Nina Kaur (Customer): It also seems correlated with higher concurrency plus longer prompts. We had a batch job that pushed longer contexts, and it got worse.

[01:38] Sofia Ivanova (Redwood): That matches what we’ve been seeing. Under mixed sequence lengths you can end up with a lagging rank, then a cancellation or disconnect happens, and the scheduler/barrier semantics can basically deadlock a tensor-parallel group.

[01:52] Elena Popov (Customer): When you say “deadlock”, you mean the GPUs are alive but no forward progress?

[01:57] Sofia Ivanova (Redwood): Exactly. The process is still up, but that TP group won’t make progress on the collective or the barrier that gates the next step.

[02:06] Dev Patel (Redwood): And the other bucket is NCCL async errors not surfacing quickly, so it looks like a hang until a higher-level timeout fires.

[02:14] Miguel Santos (Customer): We did see NCCL in logs once. But it’s not consistent.

[02:19] Sofia Ivanova (Redwood): Yeah, it won’t be. Sometimes you get a clean NCCL error, sometimes the collective just sits waiting and nobody reports it.

[02:27] Dev Patel (Redwood): Before we go deep—can you confirm current runtime version on the Dedicated cluster? From our notes it looked like 1.18.3?

[02:35] Miguel Santos (Customer): Correct, 1.18.3.

[02:38] Connor O'Brien (Redwood): And you’re pinned there currently, no auto-upgrades.

[02:41] Miguel Santos (Customer): Yes.

[02:44] Dev Patel (Redwood): OK.

[02:46] Nina Kaur (Customer): Can we talk mitigations first? Because we need to not have this happen again tomorrow.

[02:52] Dev Patel (Redwood): Yep. Immediate mitigations we’ve seen help are basically reducing the conditions that trigger the stall and making recovery faster when it happens.

[03:02] Rafael Mendes (Redwood): In practical terms: cap concurrent streaming requests per worker, reduce max sequence length on that route if you can, and set stricter load shedding so the cluster doesn’t enter overload.

[03:12] Nina Kaur (Customer): We can cap concurrency, but reducing max context is hard. It’s a product feature.

[03:18] Dev Patel (Redwood): Understood. The other workaround is shifting some traffic off TP=4 to either TP=2 or single GPU for the worst peak window, if you have enough headroom.

[03:28] Elena Popov (Customer): We tried TP=2 and latency got worse but it was more stable. We can do it as a fallback.

[03:34] Sofia Ivanova (Redwood): Also, the cancellation path: if clients disconnect a lot mid-stream, it increases the probability. Do you have client-side timeouts that cause disconnects?

[03:45] Chris Hammond (Customer): We do. Our edge has a 60 second timeout for initial token, and 30 seconds idle chunk timeout.

[03:52] Sofia Ivanova (Redwood): That idle timeout can cause a cancel right when the ranks are not aligned. Not saying it’s wrong, but it’s a factor.

[04:00] Miguel Santos (Customer): So you’re saying if we increase our idle chunk timeout it might reduce cancels?

[04:05] Sofia Ivanova (Redwood): Potentially. But we don’t want you masking a stall. Better is we fix cancellation-safe barriers, which is what’s in the upcoming patch.

[04:14] Dev Patel (Redwood): For now, we can suggest a couple knobs on our side: a) lower per-worker max in-flight streams, b) enable quicker worker recycle on suspected stall signals, and c) increase the server-side request timeout slightly so we can return a clean error rather than hold sockets open forever.

[04:30] Miguel Santos (Customer): We already recycle workers nightly. But during the incident we had to manually drain and restart.

[04:36] Rafael Mendes (Redwood): If you can do targeted recycle when you detect “no tokens emitted for N seconds,” that reduces blast radius. Not ideal, but it’s a short-term circuit breaker.

[04:47] Nina Kaur (Customer): What about NCCL env vars? We saw someone mention async error handling.

[04:53] Dev Patel (Redwood): Yes—there’s a setting that makes NCCL surface errors sooner. We can send the exact recommended values for your deployment. I don’t want to misquote it verbally, but yes that’s in our mitigation list.

[05:06] Miguel Santos (Customer): Please send it. We can test today.

[05:09] Dev Patel (Redwood): Will do.

[05:11] Connor O'Brien (Redwood): Just to level set: those mitigations reduce incidence, but they don’t eliminate the underlying failure mode.

[05:17] Nina Kaur (Customer): Right. So where are we on the actual fix? We were told “next release,” then it became “hotfix maybe.”

[05:25] Dev Patel (Redwood): Fair. Sofia, can you give the crisp status?

[05:29] Sofia Ivanova (Redwood): There are three changes landing together for TP stability:
1) Cancellation-safe barrier logic, so a disconnect won’t wedge the TP group.
2) More aggressive async error checks around collectives, so we don’t silently stall.
3) A TP-group forward-progress watchdog that quarantines a stuck group so it stops receiving work.

[05:54] Sofia Ivanova (Redwood): (1) and (2) are in review/merged. (3) is implemented and we’re tuning thresholds to avoid false positives.

[06:02] Rafael Mendes (Redwood): On SRE side, we’re also adding metrics so we can distinguish comm stall vs kernel stall vs scheduler starvation. Right now in prod it’s too ambiguous.

[06:12] Nina Kaur (Customer): The watchdog—what does it actually do? Does it restart the node?

[06:18] Sofia Ivanova (Redwood): The current behavior is: it marks the TP group unhealthy, the scheduler stops assigning new requests to it, and we trigger a controlled teardown of that group. Depending on the deployment mode, it can recycle just the worker process rather than the whole node.

[06:34] Miguel Santos (Customer): Controlled teardown meaning you kill the process?

[06:37] Sofia Ivanova (Redwood): Effectively yes, but we try to do it in a way that doesn’t corrupt shared state. It’s not a hard SIGKILL immediately unless it’s completely wedged.

[06:48] Chris Hammond (Customer): What happens to in-flight requests on that TP group?

[06:52] Dev Patel (Redwood): They’ll fail fast with a clear error. That’s the key difference: instead of hanging for minutes, we return and then your app can retry.

[07:02] Elena Popov (Customer): We can handle retries. We can’t handle stuck sockets.

[07:05] Dev Patel (Redwood): Exactly.

[07:08] Nina Kaur (Customer): But false positives would be bad, right? Like you’ll be killing workers during normal slowdowns?

[07:15] Rafael Mendes (Redwood): That’s why we’re proposing a canary with conservative thresholds first. The watchdog triggers only when there’s no forward progress for a defined interval, not just “latency is high.”

[07:27] Miguel Santos (Customer): Forward progress measured how?

[07:30] Sofia Ivanova (Redwood): Per-rank progress counters and collective completion signals. If a TP group hasn’t advanced its step counters while it has active work, that’s a stronger indicator than latency.

[07:43] Dev Patel (Redwood): We can share the metrics names and what to watch. Also we’ll have a dashboard panel for “watchdog triggers per hour” and “TP group resets.”

[07:53] Nina Kaur (Customer): OK. What’s the timeline?

[07:57] Connor O'Brien (Redwood): We can give you a 1.19.1 release candidate build as early as tomorrow. Then we’d do canary on your Dedicated cluster early next week.

[08:07] Nina Kaur (Customer): Tomorrow is good. But canary—do we have to upgrade the whole cluster at once?

[08:13] Connor O'Brien (Redwood): No. Dedicated supports partial rollout. We can take, say, 10% of workers, put them in a canary pool behind the same endpoint, and route a slice of traffic.

[08:23] Miguel Santos (Customer): We need to control which requests go to canary. Can we pin by header or something?

[08:28] Dev Patel (Redwood): We can do either percentage routing or a header-based route. If you want a clean test, we can route a specific internal client key to canary.

[08:38] Elena Popov (Customer): Header-based is easiest for us.

[08:41] Rafael Mendes (Redwood): Great. For success criteria, we should align on three things: timeout rate, stuck stream rate, and watchdog reset rate. If watchdog is triggering a ton, that’s not “fixed,” that’s just “failing fast.”

[08:56] Nina Kaur (Customer): Exactly.

[08:58] Dev Patel (Redwood): For a first gate, we’d like to see: no increase in p95 latency beyond, say, 5%, and watchdog triggers below a threshold—maybe <1 per 6 hours per canary worker. We’ll propose numbers and you can react.

[09:13] Miguel Santos (Customer): Ok but our traffic is bursty. We should define in terms of per million requests maybe.

[09:18] Rafael Mendes (Redwood): That’s fair. We can normalize.

[09:22] Sofia Ivanova (Redwood): Also, we should explicitly test the failure mode: streaming disconnects and cancellation. If you can generate some controlled cancels during canary, that helps.

[09:32] Elena Popov (Customer): We can do that with our load test harness.

[09:35] Dev Patel (Redwood): Perfect.

[09:38] Chris Hammond (Customer): I have a question. During the incident, we mitigated by shifting traffic to us-east temporarily. Is there any plan to improve eu-west capacity isolation? Because we saw it correlate with other tenants.

[09:51] Rafael Mendes (Redwood): Since you’re Dedicated, you’re isolated at the cluster level. But within your cluster, if it’s overload, you can see queueing effects that look like “noisy neighbor.” It’s basically your own burst.

[10:03] Miguel Santos (Customer): We did have a burst, yes. But we also saw weirdness after we drained one node—like things got worse.

[10:10] Sofia Ivanova (Redwood): Draining can shift group composition and increase fragmentation. If you end up with TP groups spread across nodes in a suboptimal way, or if one rank is on a slower host, you can amplify tail latency.

[10:24] Nina Kaur (Customer): Are you saying placement matters? Like rank-to-GPU mapping?

[10:28] Sofia Ivanova (Redwood): Yes, but mostly for stability we care about barriers and cancellations. Placement mainly impacts performance and skew.

[10:36] Dev Patel (Redwood): We can also set a short-term policy: avoid rebalancing TP groups during peak, and do maintenance drains in a calmer window.

[10:44] Miguel Santos (Customer): OK.

[10:46] Dev Patel (Redwood): Can I ask: when the stream hangs, do you ever see it eventually finish if you wait long enough?

[10:52] Elena Popov (Customer): Sometimes it never finishes. We’ve waited like 10 minutes in staging. In prod we don’t wait.

[10:58] Sofia Ivanova (Redwood): That’s consistent with a deadlocked barrier.

[11:02] Dev Patel (Redwood): Do you have any log snippet around that time? Like “entering barrier” or “collective all-reduce start” etc?

[11:10] Miguel Santos (Customer): We have some, but it’s messy. I can send timestamps.

[11:14] Sofia Ivanova (Redwood): Timestamps are enough if we can correlate with our side.

[11:20] Owen Phillips (Redwood): Sorry, jumping in—Owen from support. We also want to confirm: are these hangs only on streaming endpoints, or do you see non-streaming chat completions hang too?

[11:29] Elena Popov (Customer): Mostly streaming. Non-streaming tends to time out but not hang.

[11:34] Owen Phillips (Redwood): That helps. Streaming disconnects are a big trigger for the cancellation path.

[11:41] Nina Kaur (Customer): So the RC includes the cancellation fix?

[11:45] Connor O'Brien (Redwood): Yes.

[11:47] Nina Kaur (Customer): And this is runtime 1.19.1, not 1.19.0.

[11:51] Connor O'Brien (Redwood): Correct. 1.19.0 is the broader release. 1.19.1 is a targeted hotfix line for TP stability.

[11:59] Miguel Santos (Customer): What about risk? We can’t take a regression that hurts throughput.

[12:05] Sofia Ivanova (Redwood): The changes are designed to be low overhead. The watchdog checks are periodic, not per-token synchronization. The cancellation fix actually reduces weird stalls.

[12:16] Rafael Mendes (Redwood): For canary, we’ll watch throughput and GPU utilization. If we see a dip, we stop.

[12:23] Nina Kaur (Customer): Ok.

[12:25] Dev Patel (Redwood): Let’s talk about the immediate “tomorrow” problem. Today and tomorrow, until you canary the RC, I’d recommend:
- cap streaming concurrency per worker,
- consider temporarily routing the highest-context requests to TP=2 or single GPU,
- enable the NCCL async error handling setting (we’ll send exact),
- and set up an automated recycle if “no tokens for X seconds.”

[12:49] Chris Hammond (Customer): We already have client-side retries. But retries can double load.

[12:54] Rafael Mendes (Redwood): Right, so pair retries with backoff and max retry count. Otherwise you get retry storms.

[13:00] Nina Kaur (Customer): We can tune that.

[13:03] Elena Popov (Customer): What about increasing your server timeouts? Right now we get 504 at around 120 seconds.

[13:09] Dev Patel (Redwood): Increasing server timeout can reduce 504s, but it can also keep stuck work around longer. For stability, we prefer a lower timeout paired with fast failure and retry—once the fixes are in.

[13:22] Sofia Ivanova (Redwood): With the watchdog/quarantine, the “stuck” work should be cut off automatically.

[13:27] Miguel Santos (Customer): But that means more errors, right? Like you’re returning failures.

[13:31] Dev Patel (Redwood): In the rare case of a stall, yes, you’ll see an error rather than a hang. That’s a net improvement operationally.

[13:38] Nina Kaur (Customer): We agree. We need predictability.

[13:42] Dev Patel (Redwood): Great.

[13:44] Rafael Mendes (Redwood): Can we clarify on your side: is the cluster saturating GPU? Like are you at 90% util during these peaks?

[13:52] Miguel Santos (Customer): We’re around 75 to 85%. But queue depth grows, and then tail latency grows.

[13:59] Rafael Mendes (Redwood): OK, so overload conditions are plausible.

[14:03] Sofia Ivanova (Redwood): One more question: do you mix small and huge requests on the same route? Like short chat plus long RAG contexts.

[14:12] Elena Popov (Customer): Yes. It’s the same model endpoint. We pass different prompts.

[14:16] Sofia Ivanova (Redwood): That mixed workload can create fairness issues—short requests get stuck behind long ones in a TP group. We have some fairness changes in the scheduler, but the core issue here is deadlock, not just slowness.

[14:29] Nina Kaur (Customer): Understood.

[14:31] Dev Patel (Redwood): Let’s shift to canary plan details.

[14:35] Connor O'Brien (Redwood): Proposal: We deliver 1.19.1-rc tomorrow. Monday or Tuesday you give us a 2-hour window. We upgrade 10% of workers in eu-west Dedicated. We route an internal header from your load tester plus maybe 5% of real traffic. We monitor 24 hours.

[14:55] Connor O'Brien (Redwood): If stable, expand to 50% for another 24 hours, then 100%.

[15:02] Miguel Santos (Customer): What’s the rollback? Just downgrade those workers?

[15:06] Connor O'Brien (Redwood): Yes, roll back the canary pool to 1.18.3. It’s a standard Dedicated rollback.

[15:12] Nina Kaur (Customer): OK.

[15:14] Rafael Mendes (Redwood): For monitoring, we want to set up alerting specifically for: watchdog triggers, TP group resets, and “collective latency” spikes.

[15:24] Miguel Santos (Customer): Do we have access to those metrics or is it internal?

[15:29] Rafael Mendes (Redwood): We can expose the relevant ones in your Dedicated console. Some are internal but we can at least share dashboards and key indicators.

[15:38] Nina Kaur (Customer): We need to see it. We can’t run blind.

[15:41] Rafael Mendes (Redwood): Agreed.

[15:43] Dev Patel (Redwood): Sofia, can you explain in plain terms “collective latency” metric, since that’s new?

[15:49] Sofia Ivanova (Redwood): It’s basically how long an all-reduce or similar NCCL collective takes. In normal operation it’s very stable. When it spikes dramatically or goes to “no completion,” it indicates comm stall.

[16:02] Elena Popov (Customer): Is that different from GPU kernel stall?

[16:05] Sofia Ivanova (Redwood): Yes. Kernel stall would show compute kernels running long or not completing; comm stall is waiting on network/GPU interconnect.

[16:13] Miguel Santos (Customer): We saw GPU utilization drop to near zero on some nodes during the event.

[16:19] Rafael Mendes (Redwood): That’s a hallmark of comm wait or barrier wait. Compute goes idle.

[16:25] Chris Hammond (Customer): OK.

[16:27] Nina Kaur (Customer): Let’s talk about ownership and communication. We have leadership asking if Redwood is giving credits because we had SLA impact.

[16:36] Dev Patel (Redwood): I can’t authorize credits on the call, but I can coordinate with your CSM and our account team. Given it’s Dedicated and there was measurable impact, we’ll follow the process. We’ll document timeline and mitigations.

[16:51] Nina Kaur (Customer): OK, please do. This was customer-facing.

[16:55] Dev Patel (Redwood): Understood.

[16:57] Miguel Santos (Customer): Another thing: we considered self-hosting vLLM for this route because of this incident. We’d rather not, but we need confidence.

[17:06] Dev Patel (Redwood): Makes sense. The goal of the hotfix is exactly to prevent these stuck states and reduce operational load.

[17:13] Sofia Ivanova (Redwood): And to be clear, we’re not just adding a watchdog. We’re fixing the root cause path for cancellation/barriers.

[17:20] Elena Popov (Customer): Is there a way to reproduce this deterministically? Because we tried in staging and couldn’t.

[17:27] Sofia Ivanova (Redwood): It’s hard. We have a stress suite with fault injection—artificially delaying one rank, forcing cancels mid-token, and mixing sequence lengths. It’s not perfectly deterministic but it reproduces signatures.

[17:44] Miguel Santos (Customer): Could we get access to that suite?

[17:48] Sofia Ivanova (Redwood): It’s internal right now, but we can share the pattern and we can run your workload profile against it. If you provide distributions (lengths, concurrency, streaming ratio), we can set up a similar run.

[18:02] Elena Popov (Customer): OK, we can send that.

[18:05] Dev Patel (Redwood): Great, that’s an action item.

[18:07] Connor O'Brien (Redwood): On the RC: we’ll send a note with the version string and deployment steps. There will be a couple new config knobs. Defaults are conservative.

[18:18] Nina Kaur (Customer): Are we going to have to tune those knobs?

[18:21] Rafael Mendes (Redwood): Not initially. For canary we’ll keep default thresholds. If you have very long streams, we might adjust “no-progress” thresholds slightly, but we’ll do that together.

[18:33] Miguel Santos (Customer): OK.

[18:35] Dev Patel (Redwood): Let’s dig into the “stuck stream” handling. Currently, when it gets stuck, is it one request or a bunch?

[18:43] Miguel Santos (Customer): It’s a bunch. Like one node goes weird and then everything assigned there starts timing out.

[18:49] Sofia Ivanova (Redwood): That’s consistent with a TP group stuck and still accepting work. The quarantine logic prevents new work being scheduled onto a suspicious group.

[19:00] Elena Popov (Customer): So you’ll effectively drain it automatically.

[19:03] Sofia Ivanova (Redwood): Yes.

[19:05] Chris Hammond (Customer): When you quarantine, does it spill traffic to the remaining workers? Could that overload them?

[19:12] Rafael Mendes (Redwood): It will, yes, but we’d rather concentrate load on healthy workers than keep feeding a dead group. And we’ll pair it with backpressure so we fail fast if capacity is insufficient.

[19:25] Nina Kaur (Customer): That’s acceptable.

[19:28] Dev Patel (Redwood): Great.

[19:30] (crosstalk)

[19:31] Miguel Santos (Customer): One concern—if you’re failing fast, our retry could spike and cause a storm.

[19:37] Dev Patel (Redwood): Yep. We recommend configuring your retries with jitter and a cap. Also we can set a “retry-after” style response so you back off.

[19:47] Miguel Santos (Customer): That would help.

[19:49] Rafael Mendes (Redwood): We can include that guidance in the runbook we send.

[19:54] Nina Kaur (Customer): OK.

[19:56] Dev Patel (Redwood): Switching gears: What do you need from us for oncall? During the incident, were you paged by your metrics first or by your customers?

[20:05] Miguel Santos (Customer): Customers. Our internal dashboard didn’t flag it fast enough. We saw elevated latency but it wasn’t above threshold.

[20:12] Rafael Mendes (Redwood): OK, we should adjust your alerting to include “stuck stream” proxies, like “no tokens emitted.” We can help with suggested thresholds.

[20:23] Nina Kaur (Customer): Yes. We need earlier detection.

[20:27] Dev Patel (Redwood): Owen, can you coordinate with Miguel on alerting suggestions?

[20:31] Owen Phillips (Redwood): Yep, I’ll follow up after this.

[20:34] Dev Patel (Redwood): Thanks.

[20:36] Sofia Ivanova (Redwood): One more technical question: are you using function calling / tool calls? Those sometimes increase sequence variability.

[20:44] Elena Popov (Customer): Not heavily. Mostly plain chat completions.

[20:48] Sofia Ivanova (Redwood): OK.

[20:50] Nina Kaur (Customer): Are there known “avoid this” settings? Like certain optimizations that cause the hang?

[20:57] Sofia Ivanova (Redwood): There are some kernel/stream interactions we’re hardening, but we don’t have a single “turn this off” that fixes everything. The most consistent trigger is cancellation at the wrong time.

[21:09] Dev Patel (Redwood): We’ll send a short list of mitigations that have low downside.

[21:13] Nina Kaur (Customer): Great.

[21:15] Connor O'Brien (Redwood): Timeline check: Canary kickoff—do you prefer Tuesday 09:00 UTC?

[21:21] Miguel Santos (Customer): Tuesday is okay. But we need to confirm with our change board. Monday we can finalize.

[21:28] Connor O'Brien (Redwood): OK.

[21:30] Dev Patel (Redwood): Let’s capture agreed rollback triggers. From Redwood side: if p95 latency increases >10% sustained, or error rate increases >0.2% absolute on canary traffic, we roll back.

[21:43] Nina Kaur (Customer): Also if watchdog triggers are frequent. What’s “frequent”?

[21:47] Rafael Mendes (Redwood): For canary we can say: if watchdog resets exceed, say, 5 per million requests, or if we see repeated resets on the same node, we pause.

[22:00] Miguel Santos (Customer): That sounds reasonable.

[22:02] Elena Popov (Customer): And if the hang still occurs, obviously.

[22:05] Sofia Ivanova (Redwood): Yes.

[22:07] Dev Patel (Redwood): Great.

[22:09] Nina Kaur (Customer): What about communication? We need a written update to share internally.

[22:14] Dev Patel (Redwood): I’ll send a written recap after the call: symptoms, suspected causes, mitigations, and the canary plan with dates. Connor will attach RC details once ready.

[22:27] Chris Hammond (Customer): Please include an ETA for full rollout if canary is good.

[22:32] Connor O'Brien (Redwood): Assuming canary goes well: full rollout by end of next week.

[22:38] Nina Kaur (Customer): That’s acceptable.

[22:40] Miguel Santos (Customer): And if it doesn’t go well?

[22:43] Sofia Ivanova (Redwood): Then we keep the mitigations in place and we iterate quickly. But the core cancellation fix is pretty targeted; we expect it to improve.

[22:53] Rafael Mendes (Redwood): Also we’ll have better observability from the RC to pinpoint what’s left.

[23:00] Nina Kaur (Customer): OK.

[23:02] Dev Patel (Redwood): Are there any other asks from your side?

[23:06] Elena Popov (Customer): One thing: can you confirm whether the fix affects model output or determinism? We have compliance tests.

[23:13] Sofia Ivanova (Redwood): It shouldn’t. It’s scheduling and error handling, not math changes. In the worst case, if a group is reset, a request would retry and you could see minor nondeterminism due to retry timing, but the token generation algorithm is unchanged.

[23:29] Elena Popov (Customer): Ok.

[23:31] Miguel Santos (Customer): Another question: do we need to change our client timeouts? We set them because of previous latency.
